posts.title: Platforms, props and sequence: three temporary works failures with the same gap
posts.excerpt: HSE June 2026 City of London prosecution: no design and no loading calculation for temporary wooden platforms that collapsed under concrete debris. CROSS 1539: props sized for the column but existing RC slabs and beams in the load path not checked. CROSS 1479: late change from paired to single beam lifts created a temporary LTB risk under wet concrete.
posts.linkedinReady:
A temporary platform that carries debris is a temporary works item. So is a prop that lands on an existing slab. So is a construction sequence that changes after the design is issued. None of those items manage themselves.

On 15 June 2026 HSE published the outcome of a City of London case. Temporary wooden platforms used during refurbishment at Paxton House collapsed under concrete debris. Drilling operative Steve Zschoch, 60, was working beneath one of them. He fractured his neck and back. HSE found no design for the platforms and no calculation of a safe loading level. Roots Contractors Limited pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulation 16(2). Diacutt Limited pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulation 15(2). HSE restated that temporary structures must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand any foreseeable loads, inspected by a competent person, and used only for the purpose they were designed for.

CROSS Safety Report 1539 (14 May 2026): props for a column replacement were capable of taking the stated forces. There was no evidence the prop designer had checked the existing RC slabs and beams in the load path. When that check was done, the existing members were not strong enough in bending and shear. A temporary works drawing that does not close the load path through the existing structure is not a complete design.

CROSS Safety Report 1479 (13 January 2026): a filler-beam bridge deck was to be lifted in connected pairs. The contractor then planned to lift beams individually. That change created a temporary lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete. The Category II checker flagged it. Unbraced utilisation was reported as over 200 percent. Sequence is a design input.

For the TWC and TWS:

Register working platforms, debris decks and floors used as temporary stores. Debris is a live load.
Do not permit load without design, check category and permit-to-load.
Close the load path through existing slabs, beams, walls and foundations.
Treat a change of erection or lift sequence as a design change. Re-brief, re-check, re-permit.
Keep people out from under loaded temporary platforms.
Independent check category is provisional only, to be confirmed under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 15 June 2026 the Health and Safety Executive published a prosecution following the collapse of temporary wooden platforms during a refurbishment at Paxton House in the City of London. Drilling operative Steve Zschoch, 60, was working on the third floor under one of the platforms when it gave way under concrete debris that had not been cleared. He sustained fractures to his neck and back. HSE found no design for the platforms and no calculation of a safe loading level, plus a lack of direct supervision and confusion about working one team beneath another. At Westminster Magistrates Court on 11 June 2026, Roots Contractors Limited of Ewell pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulation 16(2) and was fined 19333 pounds plus 5548 costs. Diacutt Limited of Croydon pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulation 15(2) and was fined 13000 pounds plus 5548 costs. HSE restated that any temporary structure must be designed, installed and maintained to withstand foreseeable loads, used only for the purpose for which it was designed, and inspected by a competent person.

body.h: The load path through the existing structure
body.p: CROSS Safety Report 1539, published 14 May 2026, describes a column replacement at the base of a multi-storey block of flats. The existing column carried an estimated characteristic load of over 1165 kN and an estimated design load of about 1590 kN. Proposed props were capable of taking the required forces. The reporter found no evidence that the prop designer had checked the existing RC slabs and beams that would transfer load from the props. Once that check was done, those members were not strong enough in bending and shear. The reporter designed a more complex temporary works system and a written method statement. Issuing a temporary works drawing without checking the existing structure is not acceptable, regardless of drawing caveats.

CROSS Safety Report 1479, published 13 January 2026, covers an approximately 20 m span filler-beam bridge deck. Shortly before the Category II check was completed, the contractor altered the intended sequence from lifting steel beams in connected pairs to lifting them individually. That change introduced a temporary lateral-torsional buckling risk under wet concrete. The Category II checker identified the unbraced individual beams as critical. Without rotational restraint at the flange ends, utilisation was reported as over 200 percent. The designer confirmed that temporary LTB restraints were required. CROSS highlights communication between the permanent works designer, the temporary works designer and the Temporary Works Coordinator, and points to Network Rail B and S Engineering advice note EAN03/2025 on temporary conditions (September 2025).

These three records are not the same site. They are the same management gap. A working platform used to store demolition arisings is temporary works. A prop that sits on an existing slab is temporary works that includes the slab. A lift or pour sequence that differs from the design assumption is a new temporary condition. CDM 2015, HSE temporary works and structural-stability pages, and BS 5975-1:2024 all point to the same controls: appoint a TWC with authority, register the item, write a brief, design and check, inspect, permit to load, and treat change as change.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register every working platform, debris deck, crash deck and floor used as a temporary store. State the intended debris or plant load in the brief.
Do not load a platform or prop without a design, an agreed check category and a permit-to-load signed by a competent person who has seen the as-built arrangement.
Close the load path through existing slabs, beams, walls, columns and foundations. A prop capacity check that stops at the head of the prop is incomplete.
Treat a change of erection sequence, lift pairing, pour bay or striking order as a design change. Re-brief, re-check, update the method and re-issue the permit.
Keep exclusion zones under loaded temporary platforms. Two trades stacked vertically need a written arrangement.
Inspect after debris is placed, after rainfall, and after any alteration to the platform or support.
Hold permit-to-strike until the permanent works can take the load.

Independent check category is provisional only. Platforms carrying unknown debris, props on existing structure of unknown capacity, and sequence changes on bridge decks normally point to escalation, not a CAT 0 close-out.
